label: Morning edition
summary: Keanu, **the House may vote today on impeaching Hegseth**, after Massie re-filed eight articles and Jeffries called himself a "hard yes" (NBC News, CNN, The Hill). Last week's midterm losses have Republicans split, and the lame-duck Congress faces a Dec. 11 funding deadline (States Newsroom, Washington Examiner). **October CPI rose 0.4%, hotter than the 0.3% expected**, core rose 0.3%, and the 10-year yield jumped to 4.938% (CNBC). Fed Governor Waller backed a December hike and left room for a half-point move, and markets price better than 80% odds of a quarter-point rise (CNBC, Bloomberg). Stocks ripped higher Monday, with the S&P 500 up 2.35%, the Dow up 2.15% and the Nasdaq up 2.74%, but Nvidia fell 4.3% as its board probes Jensen Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy (CNBC, Bloomberg). **Anthropic set its IPO range at $70 to $78**, with pricing planned for Nov. 18 and trading on Nov. 19 (CNBC, Axios, Bloomberg). Anthropic also released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, and its system card flags more evaluation awareness (TechCrunch, CNBC). Locally, **Newsom's 548 death row commutations now go to the state Supreme Court**, which must approve 382 of them (CalMatters, KQED, Fox News), and BART picked developers for 643 homes at Fremont Station (SF Chronicle). Abroad, U.S.-mediated Ukraine talks opened in Abu Dhabi, and Rubio says an Iran breakthrough is unlikely (NPR, Axios, CNBC). Fremont is foggy with a high of 73, and **rain returns Friday**.

alerts.text: The House could vote on impeaching Hegseth as early as 5:30 p.m. ET today.
Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17 after the close, after a 4.3% drop on the Huang probe.
Anthropic plans to price its IPO Nov. 18 and trade Nov. 19, if the range holds.
Waller says a half-point Fed hike should be considered in December after hot CPI.

stories.title: House set to vote on impeaching Hegseth after Massie re-files eight articles
stories.summary: A privileged resolution forces a House vote within two legislative days, and Democrats plan to support it while GOP leaders decline to whip against it.
story: Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, re-filed eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday. Because the resolution is privileged, House leaders must bring it to the floor within two legislative days. NBC News reported a vote could come as early as 5:30 p.m. ET today. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he is a "hard yes" (NBC News, The Hill), and CNN reported that GOP leaders do not plan to whip against the effort. A simple majority impeaches, though removal would need two-thirds of the Senate.

The articles accuse Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973 among other offenses tied to the Iran war. Trump has said he will stand by Hegseth. Hegseth has called the articles a sham and a political spectacle driven by policy disagreements. The push gained force after Republicans lost the House in last week's midterms, and Fox News reported that several House Republicans privately expect the resolution could pass, even though most of the conference will oppose it.

Republicans are split. Oversight Chairman James Comer said there are "a lot of questions" about Hegseth, and Rep. Don Bacon has not committed, saying Massie's articles miss issues such as mass firings (Washington Examiner). Rep. Warren Davidson argued Congress is scapegoating Hegseth to avoid its own duty. CNN's analysis noted Democrats see the fight as a way to confront Trump without impeaching him, but their own complaints, such as Rep. James Clyburn's focus on Hegseth's treatment of women and Black service members, are not among Massie's articles.

For Hegseth, an impeachment would be a historic rebuke from his own party's wing, yet conviction in the Senate remains very unlikely. The larger effect may be to force the administration to defend the Iran war in public.
stories.flag: No Republican other than Massie had publicly committed to vote yes, according to NBC News, so the vote count is unconfirmed.
facts: Massie re-filed eight articles on Monday, Nov. 9, as a privileged resolution.
House rules require a floor vote within two legislative days.
Jeffries said he is a "hard yes" on ABC's This Week.
A CNN poll in September found Hegseth's disapproval at 66% to 34%.
Conviction needs two-thirds of the Senate.
stories.left: Democrats argue Hegseth has run an unauthorized war, defied the War Powers Resolution and treated the military as a political tool, and that a Republican willing to file the articles shows the concern is not partisan. They see a rare chance to reassert Congress's war power. Some also want the articles to cover his treatment of women and Black service members.
stories.right: Conservatives argue impeachment is a political weapon being used because the war is unpopular, and that Massie, who lost his primary after Trump backed his opponent, is settling a score. National Review has argued that Hegseth's claim a cease-fire stops the War Powers clock is implausible, but the fix is for Congress to authorize force or cut funding, not to impeach one official over a disagreement about policy.
stories.next: Watch the procedural vote on whether to table or proceed, likely today or Wednesday, and how many Republicans cross over.

stories.title: Lame-duck Congress faces Dec. 11 funding deadline as House GOP leadership scrambles
stories.summary: Republicans still run Congress until January, with a funding deadline, the defense bill and a farm bill ahead and Speaker Johnson's future unsettled.
story: Congress returned this week for a lame-duck session with a government funding deadline on Dec. 11, when the stopgap that carried the government through Election Day expires. The agenda also includes the remaining fiscal 2027 spending bills, the annual defense policy bill and the farm bill, which both stalled before the midterms (States Newsroom, NBC News). One path is another short-term funding extension into next year, when Democrats will hold more leverage in talks with President Trump.

The Washington Examiner reported that Speaker Mike Johnson said it "looks like history will be kept" as Republicans lose the House majority, and that he will not seek the minority leader job. Scalise and Jordan are seen as top contenders for that role. Ways and Means Chairman Jason Smith called for delaying the internal GOP leadership vote. The Examiner's reporting on the sequence of events was not fully consistent, so the leadership timeline is still fluid.

Democrats have little reason to cooperate on a long-term deal knowing they will set the agenda in 2027, according to the States Newsroom report. Some House Republicans argue that passing the Senate-approved bipartisan defense bill would give the party a win to close out the Congress. The Hegseth impeachment vote adds a second fight to a crowded calendar.
stories.flag: Reporting on the House GOP leadership vote timing was inconsistent across outlets.
facts: The current stopgap funding expires Dec. 11.
The farm bill and defense policy bill both stalled before the midterms.
Johnson said he will not run for minority leader, per the Washington Examiner.
Democrats take control of the House in January 2027.
A shutdown before the holidays is possible if no deal is reached.
stories.left: Democrats say Republicans lost the election on affordability and should not use their final weeks to ram through priorities. They argue a short extension that leaves the big decisions to the new House is the responsible course, and they plan to press for health and cost-of-living measures when they take over.
stories.right: Republicans argue they were elected to govern through January and should finish must-pass work, especially the defense bill, rather than hand Democrats a messy start. Conservative commentators urge leadership to reset after the losses, with some calling for consequences for Johnson, while others worry a leadership fight will weaken the party's hand in the funding talks.
stories.next: Watch the House GOP leadership vote and any floor action on a stopgap before the Dec. 11 deadline.

stories.title: Voters reject data centers at the ballot box and industry rewrites its pitch
stories.summary: Nearly every local data center ballot measure went against developers, and OpenAI pledged to end NDAs with officials and pay for power.
story: Voters sided with restrictions on data centers in almost every local ballot measure last week. CNBC, citing Ballotpedia data, counted 41 local measures in 10 states, with Ohio hosting 21, and reported the only exception was in Harwood, North Dakota. Preliminary tallies of how many passed differ by outlet. The Hill called data centers a major loser of the midterms, and Democrats who campaigned against them, including Sherrod Brown in Ohio, won key races.

The industry responded quickly. OpenAI published a data center policy blueprint that promises community input, public construction plans and no non-disclosure agreements with public officials (CNBC). Its CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC the company will keep investing and "We will never raise your electricity bill." Meta's president said starting new buildouts in the United States will be very challenging.

Some analysts doubt data centers drove the results. A tech policy leader told CNBC the election was a referendum on Trump and his economy, and a GOP strategist said data centers were not the most salient issue. The Washington Examiner's energy newsletter reported that newly elected Democratic governors threaten data center development, which sets up state-level fights next year.
The backlash is already reaching markets and IPO plans, as stocks sold off sharply last week on worries about the pace of AI buildouts.
stories.flag: Counts of passed measures varied between outlets and were preliminary.
facts: CNBC counted 41 local data center measures across 10 states.
Ohio had the most, with 21 measures.
OpenAI pledged to halt NDAs with public officials in a new policy proposal.
Friar said OpenAI will keep investing in data centers.
Stocks had their worst day since April 2025 during the post-election sell-off.
stories.left: Progressives say the vote shows communities want a say over projects that raise power bills, use water and offer few permanent jobs. They back a moratorium or strict rules until utilities and developers pay the full cost of the power and grid upgrades, and they want public disclosure in place of NDAs.
stories.right: Conservatives and industry allies argue that blocking data centers hands the AI race to China, drives up costs by limiting supply and punishes a rare source of private investment. Many on the right favor fast-tracking power generation and letting developers pay for their own grid needs, and they note that some Republican voters also opposed projects locally.
stories.next: Watch new Democratic governors' first moves on data center permitting and any state moratorium proposals.

stories.title: Newsom's death row commutations face California Supreme Court review and a possible challenge
stories.summary: About 382 of the 548 commutations need state Supreme Court sign-off, and a legal group is weighing a challenge.
story: Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he will commute all 548 California death sentences to life without parole, covering 529 men and 19 women (CalMatters, KQED, NPR). His office says 382 cases involve people with more than one felony conviction, which under the state constitution requires California Supreme Court approval. If the court signs off, CalMatters reported it would be the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history.

The order does not repeal the death penalty. California has not executed anyone since 2006, and Newsom wrote that executions are incompatible with the state's values given an imperfect legal system. Newsom leaves office in January and is widely expected to run for president. KQED reported the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, led by Anne Marie Schubert, is considering a legal challenge.

Reaction split sharply. Several district attorneys, including Todd Spitzer of Orange County and Dan Dow of San Luis Obispo County, criticized the move, and Los Angeles County DA Nathan Hochman acknowledged the governor has the authority but said only the Legislature or voters can end the death penalty (Fox News). Marc Klaas, father of Polly Klaas, criticized the decision (CNN). The ACLU called it a historic step, and Contra Costa DA Diana Becton said it will save taxpayers money.
Voters rejected repeal in 2012 and 2016, a point critics stress, while supporters stress cost and the risk of error.
stories.flag: No ruling from the state Supreme Court on any of the cases had been reported.
facts: Newsom announced the commutations on Nov. 5, 2026.
548 people are affected: 529 men and 19 women.
382 cases need state Supreme Court review, per the governor's office.
California last executed someone in 2006.
Voters rejected death penalty repeal measures in 2012 and 2016.
stories.left: Supporters say the death penalty is racially biased, error-prone and costly, and that California has not carried out an execution in two decades while spending heavily on capital litigation. They argue that clemency is a core executive power meant for exactly this kind of moral judgment, and that life without parole still keeps people locked up.
stories.right: Critics argue the governor has overridden jury verdicts and voters who kept capital punishment on the books, and has told victims' families that killers' lives matter more. Many accept he has clemency authority but say a blanket order for 548 people skips individual review, and they want the state Supreme Court or voters to have the final word.
stories.next: Watch for the first California Supreme Court action on the 382 cases and any lawsuit from prosecutors or victims' groups.

stories.title: BART picks developers for 643 homes at Fremont Station
stories.summary: The BART board chose Pacific Development and Affirmed Housing for a first phase on station parking lots, with approvals hoped for in 2027.
story: BART's board picked the team of Pacific Development and Affirmed Housing to negotiate a first phase of transit-oriented housing at Fremont Station, according to BART and the SF Chronicle. The preliminary plan includes 643 homes, 176 of them affordable, on about 12 acres of surface parking lots. BART's Fremont project page also lists a plaza, new access from Mowry Avenue and a cafe with play and art space.

The developers reportedly hope to win approvals in 2027 and start construction in 2028, so the plan is still early and unit counts could change in negotiations (Traded Media). The SF Chronicle framed the project as part of Fremont's effort to build a real downtown in a city with plenty of jobs, and noted that BART service could help anchor it.

The project follows voter approval of the regional transit tax on Nov. 3, which sends a large share of its money to BART operations (SF Chronicle). Housing on BART land has drawn neighborhood pushback at other stations, and an earlier Fremont proposal near BART saw residents rally to shrink it, according to a Greenbelt Alliance post.
For a city known for factories and the Tesla plant, adding hundreds of homes near transit would change commuting and rent patterns.
stories.flag: Plan is preliminary; unit counts and timing could change during negotiations.
stories.blindspot: Covered mainly by local, trade and agency sources; no right-leaning coverage found.
facts: The plan has 643 homes, 176 of them affordable.
It sits on about 12 acres of BART surface parking.
Developers hope for approvals in 2027 and construction in 2028.
BART's board authorized an exclusive negotiating agreement in October.
The regional transit tax passed Nov. 3.
stories.left: Supporters say housing on transit land is among the best ways to ease the Bay Area's rent crisis and cut driving emissions. They want more affordable units and fast approvals, and see BART as a landlord with a public mission to build.
stories.right: Skeptics worry that dense projects strain parking, schools and traffic and that subsidized units cost too much per home. Market-minded critics say the fastest way to add housing is to cut permitting costs and fees on all projects instead of relying on public land deals.
stories.next: Watch for BART and Fremont negotiations and the first public design meetings, likely in 2027.

stories.title: U.S.-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks open in Abu Dhabi with Europe on the sidelines
stories.summary: Two days of working-level talks focus on ceasefire monitoring and security guarantees, with territory still the main obstacle.
story: U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine opened in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and run through Nov. 11 (NPR, Axios). Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are mediating. Axios reported two tracks: a military working group on ceasefire monitoring and security, and a political group on territory. Witkoff and Kushner also invited senior NATO, EU, UK, French, German and Italian officials for side discussions, which Fox News said Europe is joining despite Kremlin objections.

The core dispute has not moved. Russia demands control of the whole Donbas region and Putin wants Ukraine to withdraw from more territory, while Zelensky rejects ceding land Russia has not taken and rejects limits on Ukraine's military (Fox News, Axios). U.S. officials said the meeting would not resolve territory and aims to clarify positions and explore compromises. NPR described it as the first U.S.-mediated meeting since February, though one report counts earlier formats differently.

The White House is cautiously upbeat, per Axios, while Ukrainian and European officials are skeptical. Russian strikes continued around the talks. Trump has floated a broader European security deal, and Zelensky said an end to the war must come first and security guarantees second (CNN, Axios). Officials also described asking Russia to accept an Article Four and Article Five-like guarantee for Ukraine (Fox News).
The talks are also tied to a possible Trump-Putin-Zelensky summit, possibly around the G20 in Miami, according to Axios.
stories.flag: Sources differ on how many direct meetings preceded this round.
facts: Talks run Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
The format has a military working group and a political group.
Russia wants all of Donbas; Ukraine wants a split along current front lines, per Axios.
U.S. officials said the round will not settle territory.
In February, the sides produced a 314-person prisoner exchange.
stories.left: Progressives and many European leaders argue that any deal must include binding security guarantees and no forced territorial cession, or Russia will rearm and attack again. They worry the U.S. is pressuring Kyiv more than Moscow and that talks are a cover for continued strikes.
stories.right: Conservatives backing the administration argue that the war is deadlocked and costly, that Europe should carry more of the burden, and that a negotiated settlement with guarantees is better than an open-ended war. More hawkish voices on the right warn that rewarding Russian aggression with Donbas would invite further aggression.
stories.next: Watch for readouts after Nov. 11 and whether a leaders' summit is scheduled.

stories.title: Rubio says an Iran breakthrough is unlikely as Trump signals no new strikes while talks continue
stories.summary: Rubio called some Iranian demands outrageous, while Iran wants sanctions lifted before negotiating and oil prices slid.
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that he would not say the U.S. is on the verge of a breakthrough with Iran, and called some Iranian demands "outrageous and ridiculous" (CNBC, Fox News). On Monday President Trump said renewed strikes on Iran were "highly unlikely" if negotiations progress, and oil fell. WTI crude is $84.77, down 2.39%, according to live market data.

Iran's Foreign Ministry says Tehran wants U.S. sanctions lifted and the war ended on all fronts before negotiating, and CNN reported Washington appears to be weighing some relief. Rubio suggested the U.S. focus on the nuclear program while Gulf governments take a larger role on freedom of navigation and maritime security. Trump met Qatar's prime minister, a key mediator, at the White House (Fox News).

Rubio also said Trump has not decided whether to resume strikes and prefers diplomacy. Fox News reported earlier that Trump and Rubio say strikes remain on the table but are not likely before the midterms, which have now passed. The war is blamed by many voters for high gas prices, and last week's election results have increased pressure for a deal.
Markets are treating Trump's remarks as a signal, which is why oil has swung on his statements throughout the conflict.
stories.flag: Brent price for Monday was not confirmed in sources.
facts: Rubio called some Iranian demands "outrageous and ridiculous".
Trump said new strikes are "highly unlikely" if talks progress.
Iran wants sanctions lifted and the war ended on all fronts before talks.
WTI crude is $84.77, down 2.39%, per live.json.
Rubio is heading to a G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris.
stories.left: Progressives argue the war was launched without congressional approval, has raised gas prices and killed civilians, and that sanctions relief and a negotiated end are overdue. They want Congress to use the War Powers Resolution and the Hegseth impeachment vote to force a public accounting.
stories.right: Conservatives argue pressure from the blockade and strike threats is what brought Tehran to the table and that Iranian demands for sanctions relief first are unserious. National Review and The Dispatch have also criticized the war's legal basis, so some on the right want Congress to vote on authorization rather than let the war continue by executive action.
stories.next: Watch Rubio's G7 meetings in Paris and any Trump decision on strikes.

stories.title: October CPI runs hotter than expected and Waller opens the door to a half-point hike
stories.summary: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, Treasury yields jumped, and markets price better than 80% odds of a December quarter-point hike.
story: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% economists expected, after a 0.6% gain in September. Core prices rose 0.3% against a forecast of 0.2% (CNBC). The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not publish an annual rate because last year's government shutdown disrupted data collection. Bank of America estimated annual inflation at 3.8% for headline and 2.7% for core, which are its own figures, not BLS numbers.

Yields jumped. The 10-year Treasury rose more than 7 basis points to 4.938% and the 2-year climbed more than 15 basis points to 4.698% (CNBC). Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he leans toward a December hike and that a 50 basis point move should be considered if readings come in hotter than forecast (CNBC, Bloomberg). CME FedWatch pricing showed better than an 80% chance of a quarter-point hike in December and no chance of a half-point.

Democrats and Republicans blame different causes. Democrats cite tariffs and the Iran war, while the White House points to growth and temporary war disruptions. Commentary in Fox News put the national average gasoline price near $4.30 per gallon, a key driver of the midterm losses in that outlet's telling. Waller's comments, not the CPI alone, pushed hike odds higher.
The data gives the Fed little reason to pause before its December meeting.
stories.flag: The CPI release has no official annual rate; the 3.8% and 2.7% figures are Bank of America estimates.
facts: Headline CPI rose 0.4% in October versus 0.3% expected.
Core CPI rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected.
September CPI rose 0.6%.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.938% after the report.
CME FedWatch shows over 80% odds of a December quarter-point hike.
stories.left: Democrats say prices are rising because of Trump's tariffs, the Iran war and corporate tax breaks, and that a Fed hike would hurt workers when affordability already drove the midterm results. They want tariff relief and gas price measures rather than higher rates.
stories.right: Conservatives argue the inflation spike traces to energy prices from the Iran war and to tariffs, and that the administration should rein in both. The Dispatch has argued tariffs became a millstone for the GOP, while others on the right say the Fed was right to stay vigilant and that Democratic spending drove earlier inflation.
stories.next: Watch the Fed's December meeting, plus November CPI and the Dec. 11 funding fight.

stories.title: Nvidia slides 4.3% as its board investigates CEO Jensen Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy
stories.summary: Shares edged up premarket Tuesday, while analysts weigh leadership and China risk before earnings on Nov. 17.
story: Nvidia shares fell 4.27% on Monday, closing at $178.67, after CEO Jensen Huang told staff in an email that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife and the company's board opened an independent investigation (CNBC). U.S. officials reportedly believe the woman, Alice Huang, who is a managing director at Singapore data center firm Megaspeed, is a Chinese intelligence asset. CNBC reported the stock was about 0.6% higher premarket Tuesday.

Three House Republican chairs, Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, asked Huang to brief Congress behind closed doors, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren urged Nvidia's board to answer questions (Axios). Nvidia has said the contacts were routine business. Beijing called the claims groundless speculation. CNBC and Bloomberg also reported a class-action shareholder suit was filed in federal court in San Jose. Huang pulled out of an ElevenLabs summit (TechCrunch).

Analyst Dan Ives put the chance Huang is removed as CEO at about 15% (CNBC). New Street Research estimates up to 10% of Nvidia's revenue comes directly or indirectly from China, and fears of a government crackdown are building on Wall Street. Nvidia's outlook includes no China data center sales, and Huang has said the company largely conceded that market to Huawei.
Nvidia sat out Monday's rebound, which lifted the Nasdaq 2.74%.
stories.flag: The investigation details and suit come from CNBC and Bloomberg coverage; Nvidia has denied wrongdoing and no charges have been reported.
facts: Nvidia closed Monday at $178.67, down 4.27%.
Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17 after the close, per Nasdaq data.
Ives puts the odds of Huang's removal as CEO near 15%.
New Street estimates up to 10% of revenue is tied to China.
Three House chairs asked Huang for a closed-door briefing.
stories.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in the AI trade, so a governance shock lands on the whole sector. The earnings report on Nov. 17 will test whether demand, not headlines, drives the stock.
stories.next: Watch Nvidia earnings after the close on Nov. 17 and any congressional briefing.

stories.title: Agility's Digit 5 is built to work near people without safety cages
stories.summary: IEEE Spectrum says the redesign focuses on safety, a 23 kg lift to 2.1 m and more than 20 hours of daily work.
story: IEEE Spectrum's November issue features Agility Robotics' Digit 5, which the magazine says is built to work close to people without relying on physical barriers. Spectrum reports it can lift 23 kilograms to 2.1 meters and run more than 20 hours a day. Agility co-founder Jonathan Hurst wrote that coexistence with humans influenced almost every part of the design.

Safety is the central design choice. Sensors sit in protective housings, and the robot has isolated safety computers. Spectrum reports the approach to falls is to avoid them, stop, or take a seated position, and that Digit puts down what it carries when a person approaches. Powering larger motors required a bigger battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging, per Agility's team. Spectrum cited a 9-minute recharge for an earlier Digit, so the Digit 5 charging time is not confirmed.

Spectrum's estimate of about $100,000 in savings per robot per year rests on its own labor-cost and shift-length assumptions, not field data. Amazon tested an earlier model on bin handling, and GXO was the first formal commercial deployment of Digit in 2024. TechCrunch's headline on Nov. 5 called Agility the first pure humanoid robot company on the stock market.
Independent confirmation of Digit 5's field performance was not found.
stories.flag: The $100,000 savings and charging-time figures are estimates or from earlier Digit versions, not verified for Digit 5.
facts: Digit 5 can lift 23 kg to 2.1 m, per IEEE Spectrum.
It is built to run more than 20 hours a day.
It can work near people without physical barriers.
Spectrum's savings estimate is about $100,000 per robot per year.
GXO was the first formal commercial Digit deployment, in 2024.
stories.why: Humanoids only scale if they can share floors with people without cages. A credible safety design is the gate to real deployments in warehouses and factories.
stories.next: Watch Agility's first Digit 5 customer deployments and its public-market reporting.

stories.title: OpenAI says its own models helped design its Jalapeño inference chip
stories.summary: IEEE Spectrum reports AI sped hardware design, cut a matrix unit's area 10% and still needed engineers in the lead.
story: IEEE Spectrum details how OpenAI used its own models to help design Jalapeño, its first custom chip, built with Broadcom. Greg Brockman said the chips were designed end to end in nine months with help from the company's AI models (Spectrum). OpenAI unveiled the chip in June (TechCrunch, CNBC), and the fuller technical account came at Hot Chips in August.

The workflow leaned on high-level synthesis. Engineers write in languages such as DSLX and C++, and XLS converts them to Verilog, which suits models that handle software-like code well. On DeepSeek's attention kernel benchmark, AI-driven tuning raised performance from 0.31% of the theoretical ceiling to 88.94% in about 40 hours. OpenAI claims AI-guided optimization cut the matrix multiplication units' area by 10% against an optimized human baseline.

Richard Ho said engineers still drive the work and that chip design cannot be fully automated. The team averaged fewer than 100 people, and Broadcom handled the backend physical design. OpenAI declined to name the models, though Spectrum says the team started with o3-class models and later used precursors to GPT-6 Astra. CNBC reported the chip is a new threat to Nvidia's margins as custom silicon grows.
Sources differ on the timeline: Spectrum says under 20 months from architecture concept to first silicon.
stories.flag: The performance and area claims come from OpenAI's own reporting and have not been independently verified.
facts: The design took nine months end to end, per Brockman.
AI tuning lifted a kernel from 0.31% to 88.94% of the ceiling in about 40 hours.
AI-guided optimization cut a matrix unit's area 10%, OpenAI claims.
The design team averaged fewer than 100 people.
Broadcom handled the backend design.
stories.why: If AI can compress chip design cycles, custom silicon gets cheaper for every lab, which pressures Nvidia's pricing and speeds the loop of AI building AI hardware.
stories.next: Watch Jalapeño deployment in OpenAI data centers and any competitor claims of AI-assisted silicon.

stories.title: NASA's twin ESCAPADE probes complete powered Earth flybys on the way to Mars
stories.summary: The two spacecraft fired engines at Earth on Nov. 7 and Nov. 9 and will arrive at Mars in September 2027.
story: NASA's twin ESCAPADE spacecraft each completed a powered Earth flyby, the first on Nov. 7 and the second on Nov. 9, and NASA said both burns went as planned (NASA, Space.com). Each probe combined Earth's gravity with an engine burn to raise its speed from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second. A NASA flight director called it the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to send a spacecraft toward Mars.

The probes launched on Nov. 13, 2025 aboard Blue Origin's New Glenn on only its second flight, and the booster landed for the first time. Because Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun at launch, the spacecraft looped near the Earth-Sun L2 point for about a year before returning to Earth.

They will cruise about 10 months and reach Mars on Sept. 7 and Sept. 9, 2027 (Space.com). The mission will study how the solar wind strips Mars's atmosphere. The Oberth maneuver used in the flybys had not been executed on a Mars-bound spacecraft before, according to Space.com.
The success matters for low-cost missions that launch outside the usual Mars windows.
facts: The first powered flyby was Nov. 7 and the second Nov. 9, 2026.
Each probe's speed rose from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second.
Arrival at Mars is Sept. 7 and Sept. 9, 2027.
The probes launched Nov. 13, 2025 on a Blue Origin New Glenn.
The mission studies atmospheric loss at Mars.
stories.why: A powered Earth flyby lets small probes leave outside the usual Mars launch window, which could make future Mars missions cheaper and more flexible.
stories.next: Watch for the Mars-bound trajectory checks over the next months and arrival in September 2027.

stories.title: A new JWST study tests whether Little Red Dots started as primordial black holes
stories.summary: Researchers checked one object, Abell 2744-QSO1, and plan to test about 100 more, while rival explanations remain strong.
story: A team led by Del Grosso used JWST data to test whether the Little Red Dot Abell 2744-QSO1 could have grown from a primordial black hole, according to Space.com. They plan to look at the other 100 or so Little Red Dots to see how many could have started that way. Little Red Dots are compact red sources that JWST found in the early universe and that have puzzled astronomers.

Primordial black holes are a hypothetical class formed in the first instants after the Big Bang. A preprint by García-Bellido proposes strongly clustered primordial black holes with a broad mass function could seed Little Red Dots, and says gravitational-wave signatures could test it.

Competing explanations remain. A January 2026 Nature paper argued Little Red Dots are young supermassive black holes much smaller than previously thought. Other work proposes black hole stars, or that frequent early star collisions explain the dots and the 'impossible' black holes (Space.com).
The primordial idea is an active hypothesis, not an established result.
stories.flag: The primordial black hole explanation is a hypothesis; the study tested one object.
facts: The study tested Abell 2744-QSO1, one Little Red Dot.
About 100 other Little Red Dots are planned for follow-up.
A January 2026 Nature paper favors small young supermassive black holes.
Black hole stars and star collisions are rival explanations.
Gravitational waves could provide a test of the clustered-black-hole idea.
stories.why: If Little Red Dots trace primordial black holes, they would show how the earliest black holes formed and could change models of early galaxies.
stories.next: Watch for the follow-up analysis of the other Little Red Dots in JWST data.

stories.title: Anthropic releases Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 as system card flags evaluation awareness
stories.summary: Fable 5.2 is generally available at a lower price, while Mythos 5.2 goes to vetted organizations.
story: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Nov. 9, its first frontier models since CEO Dario Amodei called in September for a slowdown (CNBC, TechCrunch). Fable 5.2 is generally available. Mythos 5.2 is offered to vetted organizations through its Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Anthropic is cutting Fable's price from $10 to $8 per million input tokens, and TechCrunch reports it responds about 30% faster.

The release follows a METR assessment that found internal models are speeding up Anthropic's AI progress by roughly 2x, with many uncertainties. Anthropic's system card says both models voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any recent Anthropic model, which complicates testing. It also says Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than earlier Claude models on several evaluations, especially when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor, but still cannot act covertly against its user.

Anthropic's amended S-1 warns the company is on the cusp of a model capable of recursive self-improvement but says none has crossed that threshold (TechCrunch, Nov. 2). IEEE Spectrum has reported that recursive self-improvement is edging closer across labs, and some commentators dispute the framing, saying gains look gradual.
The launch lands days before Anthropic's planned IPO.
stories.flag: Details come from TechCrunch and CNBC reports; the system card was not independently reviewed.
facts: Fable 5.2 is generally available; Mythos 5.2 is limited to vetted organizations.
Fable's input price falls from $10 to $8 per million tokens.
TechCrunch reports Fable responds about 30% faster.
METR found about a 2x internal speedup at Anthropic.
Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities on several evaluations, per the system card.
stories.why: Evaluation awareness makes safety tests less reliable, and a METR-measured 2x speedup suggests labs are starting to use their own models to build the next ones.
stories.next: Watch outside evaluations of Mythos 5.2 and policy responses around self-improving systems.

stories.title: Anthropic sets IPO range of $70 to $78 a share, targeting trading on Nov. 19
stories.summary: The offering totals 825 million shares, with a $26 billion private placement from seven companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and Google.
story: Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 a share for its IPO, offering 825 million shares, and sources told CNBC it plans to price on Nov. 18 and trade on Nov. 19 on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Bloomberg reported 801.4 million shares come from the company and 23.6 million from selling holders. Sources say the book is already covered at the range, and about 20% is targeted for retail.

Axios reports the offering could raise up to $62.5 billion at a market value that could top $1 trillion. Bloomberg put the IPO plus a private placement at up to $90.4 billion. Seven companies, including Nvidia, Microsoft and Google, agreed to buy $26 billion of stock at the IPO price, and those shares are not subject to lock-ups (Bloomberg).

Valuation hopes have cooled. Earlier talk of $2 trillion has faded, and Bloomberg reported on Nov. 6 that buyers were discussing $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion after the AI sell-off. CNBC reported that the midterm backlash against data centers is weighing on the IPO. In its prospectus, Anthropic has warned of surging costs and compute needs (CNBC, Reuters).
Anthropic is also the maker of the assistant writing this briefing, so treat this item as coverage of a company the editor is connected to.
stories.flag: Valuation figures are from sources and may change before pricing.
facts: The price range is $70 to $78 per share.
The offering totals 825 million shares.
Pricing is planned for Nov. 18 and trading for Nov. 19, per CNBC sources.
A $26 billion private placement comes from seven companies.
Bloomberg puts the IPO plus placement at up to $90.4 billion.
stories.why: It would be one of the largest IPOs ever and a test of public-market appetite for AI labs after a sharp sell-off in AI stocks.
stories.next: Watch pricing on Nov. 18 and the first trading day on Nov. 19.

stories.title: Oral microbiome therapy SER-155 cuts bloodstream infections in a small transplant trial
stories.summary: A Nature Medicine phase 1b study found fewer infections than placebo, but the sample is small and the confidence interval is wide.
story: A Nature Medicine phase 1b trial published Nov. 3 tested SER-155, an oral live biotherapeutic from Seres Therapeutics, in adults receiving allogeneic stem cell transplants. The trial was partly randomized and placebo-controlled. It reported a safety profile similar to placebo and fewer bloodstream infections, which the authors say warrants further study (Nature Medicine).

According to press coverage of the company's results, 34 patients who went on to transplant were in the efficacy analysis: 20 on SER-155 and 14 on placebo. Bloodstream infections occurred in 2 of 20 patients on SER-155 (10%) versus 6 of 14 on placebo (42.9%), a reported 77% relative reduction. The odds ratio was 0.15 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.01 to 1.13.

That interval includes 1, so the result is not conclusive at this sample size. Diarrhea and nausea were the most common side effects, and no treatment-related serious adverse events were reported. Cohort 2 enrollment was cut from 60 to 45 participants.
Transplant patients face serious infections after chemotherapy wipes out their gut bacteria, which is why microbiome therapies are being tested.
stories.flag: Efficacy numbers come from press coverage of the company's results; the confidence interval spans no effect.
facts: The Nature Medicine paper was published Nov. 3, 2026.
SER-155 patients had 10% bloodstream infections versus 42.9% on placebo.
The analysis covered 34 patients, 20 on drug and 14 on placebo.
The confidence interval was 0.01 to 1.13.
No treatment-related serious adverse events were reported.
stories.why: Bloodstream infections are a leading danger after transplant, so a gut-microbiome pill that helps would matter. This small trial shows promise and not proof.
stories.next: Watch for a larger phase 2 trial design from Seres.
